tip: 'Consertar' means to fix or repair: 'ele conserta computadores'. Do not confuse it with 'concerto', a concert.
'À' is 'a' plus 'a' (to plus the) written as one word: 'à noite' means at night.
The present tense in Portuguese often translates as the present continuous in English: 'procuro' = I'm looking for.
'Pedir' means to order or ask for and is irregular: 'eu peço', 'vocês pedem'.
'Violão' is the Brazilian word for acoustic guitar. 'Guitarra' in Brazil refers to an electric guitar.
'Gastar com' means to spend on; 'com' is the usual pairing: 'gastamos com transporte'.
An adjective plus 'demais' means too or excessively: 'caro demais' = too expensive.
In Brazil the object pronoun usually goes before the verb: 'pode me ajudar' (can you help me), not 'ajudar-me' as in Portugal.
No helper word like English 'do' for questions: 'você trabalha' keeps plain statement order and rising intonation makes it a question.
In Brazil 'chegar' normally takes 'em' for places, not 'a' as in European Portuguese: 'chego no trabalho'.
'O dia inteiro' means all day long, literally the whole day.
'Casa' meaning 'home' drops the article: 'para casa' is 'homeward'. Add one and 'a casa' becomes a specific house.
Think of 'a gente' as 'us folks': singular verb form, plural meaning. 'A gente quer pizza' = we want pizza.
'A gente' (we, informal) takes the singular verb form: 'a gente fala', not 'a gente falamos'.
'Gostar' takes 'de' before what you like: 'gostamos de caminhar'. English 'like' has no preposition, but drop 'de' here and the sentence breaks.
'Trocar' means to swap or exchange: 'troco ideias com os colegas' = I trade ideas with them.
'Fica' means 'is located': 'onde fica o restaurante'. Brazilians reach for 'ficar', not 'estar', for where a place sits.
'Ir' plus a verb is the everyday future: 'vou fazer compras' means 'I'm going to shop'. It beats the one-word future in speech.
Do not mix up 'vir', to come, as in 'podem vir', with 'ver', to see. One letter apart, two different verbs.
Buildings and landmarks can take 'ser' for location: 'o hotel é perto da praia'. Location is not automatically 'estar'.
'Onde tem' uses 'tem' for 'there is/are' where textbooks write 'há': 'onde tem um restaurante' is 'where is there a restaurant'.
'Marmita' is a very Brazilian concept – a homemade meal in a container that you take to work or school. It's a huge part of daily life.
'Participar de' means 'to participate in' or 'to be part of'. In Brazil, 'de' is used instead of 'em' after this verb.
Portuguese often uses 'com' plus a noun where English uses an -ly adverb: 'com paciência' = patiently.
'Ir de' + transport: 'ir de ônibus' = go by bus. No article needed after 'de' for transport.
'Dos' is 'de' plus 'os' fused into one word: 'o mais velho dos irmãos' means 'the oldest of the brothers'.
Marital status normally takes 'ser', not 'estar': 'sou casado'. Portuguese treats it as who you are, not a passing condition.
'Tomar café da manhã' means 'to have breakfast'. 'Tomar', to drink, also covers this meal in Brazilian Portuguese.
'Começar a' plus a verb means to start doing something; the 'a' is required: 'começo a trabalhar'.
'Estou com fome' is literally 'I'm with hunger': body states normally use 'estar com' plus a noun, not a direct adjective.
